clue.text: Son gets in a stew where trouble flares up

indicators.note: the son is said to get inside the stew, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a hotpot is a meat and potato stew, as in Lancashire hotpot
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A boy lands himself in trouble, in a stew, at a place where things kick off.
explanation.walkthrough: A hotpot is a Lancashire stew of meat topped with sliced potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotspot is a place of conflict or unrest where violence tends to erupt.

clue.text: Bully hero of the Trojan War

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to bully or harangue
second meaning: ..., Trojan prince killed by Achilles in the Iliad

explanation.walkthrough: The verb comes from the hero's name, once used of a swaggering bully.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trojan champion of Homer's Iliad lent his name to a verb meaning to browbeat.

clue.text: Gave inside information to head on school sports day

parts.note: a tip is the end or head of something
PE is physical education at school

explanation.surface: Someone passed a secret to the headteacher at the school sports day.
explanation.definitionFit: To tip someone off is to give them a private warning or hint.

clue.text: Tailor tried shop inspiring love for the cloth

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the jumble takes the letter inside it
to tailor is to alter or refashion, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A tailor's shop that has tried to win affection for clerical dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' is the clergy collectively; the tailoring surface makes it look like fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth is an idiom for the clergy as a body, from their distinctive dress.

clue.text: Doughnut, say, consumed by doctor usually

indicators.note: the answer is eaten up inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A doughnut, the kind a doctor usually eats.
explanation.walkthrough: A doughnut is the everyday example of a torus.
explanation.definitionFit: A torus is the ring shape in geometry, of which a ring doughnut is an example.

clue.text: Current Liverpool ground missing a part of pitch

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current

indicators.note: missing tells us the named letter is left out of the ground's name

parts.note: Anfield is the stadium of Liverpool FC
the letter A itself

explanation.surface: Liverpool's present stadium apparently lacking a section of its playing surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like an adjective meaning present-day, but it is I, the electrical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket and baseball the infield is the area of the playing field nearest the batter.

clue.text: Criminal in casino pockets million, but he can't get off

indicators.note: the scrambled letters pocket, or hold inside, the abbreviation
criminal implies something bent, so the letters are twisted round

explanation.surface: A crook in a casino pockets a million but cannot escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't get off' suggests getting away with the crime; it means can't get off to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: An insomniac is someone who habitually cannot fall asleep.

clue.text: Osaka's first service returned in game

indicators.note: returned says the letters come back the other way
the first letter of the word only

parts.note: the RAF, the Royal Air Force, is an armed service

explanation.surface: A tennis match in Osaka where the first serve is returned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' and 'returned' paint tennis; service is the armed forces here.
explanation.definitionFit: Faro is an old gambling card game in which players bet on the banker's cards.

clue.text: Expulsion of English diplomatic group

parts.note: a mission is a body of diplomats sent abroad

explanation.surface: A British diplomatic delegation being thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: Emission is the sending out or discharge of something, such as gas or light.

clue.text: Right plugs he noted going wrong? Remove from power

indicators.note: the letter plugs a gap inside the rearranged letters
going wrong means the letters go astray into a new order

explanation.surface: A political observer notes a regime faltering and calls for its overthrow.
explanation.definitionFit: To dethrone is to depose a ruler, taking away their position of authority.

clue.text: Italian island cold before 01/04

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
read as letters 01 to 04 of month 04, April: its first four letters

explanation.surface: A chilly spell before April Fools' Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 01/04 looks like the date 1 April, but it is read as letters one to four of the fourth month, APRIL, giving APRI.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is a well-known island in the Bay of Naples off southern Italy.

clue.text: Control a section of Hertfordshire's train tracks

indicators.note: section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone takes charge of part of a county's railway line.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is self-control or the act of keeping something in check.

clue.text: Magical words in poem, as seen in translation

indicators.note: a translation renders words in a new form, so these letters are rearranged into another order

explanation.surface: A spell found in a verse, as it appears when rendered into another language.
explanation.definitionFit: Ali Baba's cave opens to this phrase, the classic magic password of the Arabian Nights tale.

clue.text: Revolutionary painter with Saint Nicholas in Russia?

indicators.note: revolutionary hints at turning round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is the crossword's stock painter

explanation.surface: An artist with Saint Nicholas, possibly in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' fits the 1917 setting but here it just turns the pieces round.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas II was the last emperor of Russia, so the question mark marks him as an example of the title.

clue.text: What cleric gives, or a bishop: the answer to a problem

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
a solution answers a problem

explanation.surface: Asking whether a priest or a bishop holds the key to a difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest grants absolution, the formal forgiveness of sins after confession.

clue.text: Idiot and former PM is a comic figure

parts.note: a charlie is British slang for a fool
Gordon Brown was UK Prime Minister 2007-10

explanation.surface: A jibe that a fool and an ex-premier together make a figure of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: Calling someone a 'right charlie' is British for calling them a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Brown is the hapless hero of the Peanuts comic strip by Charles Schulz.

clue.text: Fixes crimson robes after taking off diamonds

parts.note: crimson is a shade of red

indicators.note: the named letter is taken off the robes

parts.note: to robe is to dress, so robes means dresses
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: Someone sorts things out by removing their jewels from red gowns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robes' reads as a noun, but it is the verb, dresses.
explanation.definitionFit: To redress a wrong is to remedy or put it right.

clue.text: Rickety place where peacekeepers keep their horses?

definitions.text: place where peacekeepers keep their horses?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, playful: a ..., a stable belonging to the United Nations peacekeepers

explanation.walkthrough: The UN, the United Nations, sends peacekeeping forces; split the answer UN STABLE for the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unstable is shaky and likely to fall or collapse.

clue.text: Might one take the inhabitants of a colony for lunch?

definitions.text: Might one take the inhabitants of a colony for lunch?

parts.words: Might one take the inhabitants of a colony for lunch?
parts.note: the colony is one of insects, not settlers, and the creature eats them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Colony' suggests settlers being taken out to lunch; it is an ant colony, eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: An anteater is a long-snouted mammal that feeds on ants and termites from their nests.

clue.text: One won't transmit current note about music director

parts.note: N for note, as in N.B.
on means about, as in a talk on a subject
a conductor directs an orchestra

explanation.surface: A memo concerning the orchestra's conductor, who apparently refuses to broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: An insulator, a material that does not let electricity or heat pass through it.

clue.text: Develop gun taken out of its sheath

indicators.note: the outer letters of the word are its sheath, so they come off

parts.note: a revolver is a handgun

explanation.surface: A weapon being drawn from its holster.
explanation.definitionFit: To evolve is to develop gradually over time.

clue.text: Politician on the right road turned up decay

indicators.note: in a down answer, turned up means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a Tory is a Conservative, a party of the political right

explanation.surface: A right-wing politician arriving on the street, with signs of rot.
explanation.walkthrough: TORY is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry rot is a fungal decay that crumbles timber in buildings.

clue.text: Digits in two sets? Just the odd numbers

indicators.note: only letters in odd positions, first, third, fifth and seventh, are kept

explanation.surface: Splitting digits into two groups and keeping only the odd numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digits' and 'numbers' pull towards arithmetic; the digits are on the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Toes are the digits of the foot, as fingers are those of the hand.

clue.text: Note seen in bar in South East: 50 per cent off milk shake

parts.note: SE is the compass abbreviation

indicators.note: half the letters are dropped, leaving the first half of the word

parts.note: to quaver is to tremble or shake

explanation.surface: Something spotted in a pub in south-east England, a half-price milkshake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, but here it is the bar of music in which a note sits.
explanation.definitionFit: A semiquaver is a sixteenth note in music, half the length of a quaver.

clue.text: Drive starts off in Motherwell, passing East Lothian

indicators.note: the starts, or first letters, of the next words are taken

explanation.surface: A motoring route from Motherwell through East Lothian in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Motherwell is a town and East Lothian a county in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to drive or push something forward.

clue.text: Commanding officer with case for detective Morse, say

parts.note: CO is the military abbreviation

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, first and last letters

explanation.surface: A senior officer working on a case with Inspector Morse.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse is the TV detective, but here Morse is a code.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse code, of dots and dashes, is an example of a code.

clue.text: Funny pub's motto is something drinkers say

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd or out of order, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: An amusing slogan on a pub wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A toast urging everyone to drain their glasses.

clue.text: Lazy person riled when exercising

indicators.note: exercising puts the letters through their paces, moving them into a new order

explanation.surface: A couch potato who gets annoyed whenever made to work out.
explanation.definitionFit: An idler is someone who avoids work and wastes time.

clue.text: Students putting away starter — they make bread

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is put aside

parts.note: learners are students

explanation.surface: Pupils clearing away the first course, who then go on to bake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' suggests baking; it is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, so wage earners are those who bring it in.

clue.text: Clement I has extremes of emotion during religious fast

indicators.note: these letters fall within the fast, so they go inside it

parts.note: Lent is the Christian period of fasting before Easter

indicators.note: only the first and last letters of the word are used

explanation.surface: Pope Clement I showing great feeling during Lent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clement I' reads as a pope's name, but 'Clement' is the definition and 'I' a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement means merciful or mild, as a lenient judge is.
